pos: n. (the Venetian university city whose Aristotelian faculty trained a generation of reformers and whose Averroist school was the seedbed of Italian unbelief)
etymology: From Latin Patavium, a Veneti town on the Brenta, of pre-Roman origin.
biblical_def: Padua held the second university of Italy, founded in 1222 and from 1405 under Venetian government, which protected it from Roman interference and made it the freest faculty in Catholic Europe. Protestants could take degrees there when they could take them nowhere else in Italy. Its medicine and natural philosophy were the best in the West, and its chair of logic ran a strongly Aristotelian and in part Averroist line, holding by philosophical argument propositions the church condemned, including the eternity of the world and the mortality of the individual soul. Padua therefore has a double character in this dictionary. It educated men the Reformed churches needed, among them a long file of English, Scottish, Polish and German students who came for law, medicine and Greek. It also produced the most sophisticated unbelief in sixteenth-century Europe, the school from which the Italian rationalists and in part the antitrinitarians came. The same freedom served both. The dictionary does not treat that as an argument against learning; it treats it as proof that a university cannot supply what only the word and Spirit give.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines philosophy as the knowledge of natural causes and effects; reason as the faculty of deducing inferences; a faculty as the professors of a science; immortality as exemption from death; and learning as acquired knowledge.
webster_full: PHILOSOPHY, n. Literally, the love of wisdom; the knowledge of the phenomena or effects of nature, and of the causes which produce them.
REASON, n. That intellectual power or faculty which is employed in deducing consequences from premises, or in drawing inferences.
FACULTY, n. The body of professors or instructors in a university, or in one of its departments.
IMMORTALITY, n. Exemption from death and annihilation; life destined to endure without end.
LEARNING, n. The knowledge of principles or facts received by instruction or study; acquired knowledge or ideas in any branch of science or literature.
scriptures: But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness;
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
corruption_summary: Venetian university city whose protected Aristotelian faculty trained reformers and produced the most sophisticated unbelief of sixteenth-century Europe.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the assumption, still common, that enough intellectual freedom will deliver a population to the truth. Padua had the freedom and delivered both results at once. Paul had already seen what a trained mind does with a crucified God, and he did not adjust the message to meet it: “But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness” (1Co 1:23). The obstacle at Padua was not insufficient evidence. Paul states the deeper reason, that natural capacity is the wrong instrument for the object: “But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God” (1Co 2:14).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, and it is not anti-intellectual. Scripture warns against a particular kind of philosophy, the sort that operates as a tradition independent of Christ, “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men” (Col 2:8), while the dictionary gladly owns the logic, Greek and medicine Padua taught. The sanctifying instrument is named by Christ, and it is not a syllabus: “Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth” (Joh 17:17). Reformers who had sat under Paduan Aristotelians used what they learned and submitted it; the Paduan rationalists used the same training and submitted nothing.

pos: n. (the Venetian city on the Adige whose bishop Gian Matteo Giberti made it the model diocese of the Catholic Reformation)
etymology: From Latin Verona, a city of the Veneti or Cenomani, the name of uncertain origin.
biblical_def: Verona stands on the Adige where the Brenner road comes down into the plain, and was Venetian from 1405. Its place in this dictionary belongs to one bishop. Gian Matteo Giberti, bishop from 1524, resigned the papal datary and actually resided in his see, which almost no Italian bishop did; he visited every parish, examined the clergy, enforced preaching and catechising, set up a press that printed the Greek fathers, kept a household of scholars, and left constitutions that Carlo Borromeo later copied at Milan and Trent largely adopted. He also hunted evangelicals. The dictionary records Verona as the strongest answer the Roman church had to the Reformation, and takes it seriously. Giberti proved that the abuses the Reformers named — absentee bishops, illiterate priests, no preaching, no catechism — could be corrected without conceding a single point of doctrine. That is exactly why the Reformation was never finally about abuses. A diocese may be clean, orderly, preached to and catechised, and still teach a man that he is justified in part by what he does.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a diocese as the circuit of a bishop's jurisdiction; residence as the act of dwelling in a place; visitation as the act of a superior inspecting a church; discipline as the enforcement of rules; and doctrine as that which is taught.
webster_full: DIOCESE, n. The circuit or extent of a bishop's jurisdiction; an ecclesiastical division of a kingdom or state.
RESIDENCE, n. The act of abiding or dwelling in a place for some continuance of time; the place of abode.
VISITATION, n. The act of visiting; the object of visits; a judicial visit or examination of a corporation or church.
DISCIPLINE, n. Instruction and government; the rules and regulations by which a church is governed and its members corrected.
DOCTRINE, n. Whatever is taught; principles or positions in any science; the act of teaching; whatever is laid down as true by an instructor.
scriptures: Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Gal 2:16

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
corruption_summary: Venetian city whose bishop Giberti made it the model reformed diocese of the sixteenth century, proving abuses could be cured without conceding doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the belief that the Reformation was a protest about clerical standards which better management could have answered. Verona is the refutation. Giberti gave his people resident clergy, examinations, visitations, catechism and preaching, and printed the fathers at his own press, and he burned the books of those who said a sinner is accepted by faith alone. The dictionary therefore insists on the material point: “Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28). No amount of order in a diocese answers that sentence, and no disorder refutes it.

The second paragraph names what the dictionary gladly learns from Giberti, since the Reformers themselves learned it. Jehoshaphat's teaching mission is the Old Testament model of visitation that Giberti practised and Reformed churches imitated: his men “went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people” (2Ch 17:9). Paul makes a minister's competence consist in holding the deposit so as to teach and to answer, “that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9). What Verona lacked was not energy but the article Paul twice repeats, that “by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified” (Gal 2:16).

pos: n. (the Venetian city named in 1538 as the second site for the general council, and the meeting place of the antitrinitarian collegium of the fifteen-forties)
etymology: From Latin Vicetia or Vicentia, a Veneti settlement, the name from vicus, a village.
biblical_def: Vicenza is a Venetian city between Verona and Padua, and it carries two entries in the history of the sixteenth century. In 1538, after the Mantua attempt collapsed, Paul the Third named Vicenza as the site of the general council; legates were sent, almost no bishops came, and the council was prorogued indefinitely. More consequentially, Vicenza is the traditional location of a secret collegium of about forty men said to have met around 1546 to discuss the Trinity, and from which, by the usual account, Lelio Sozzini, Giorgio Biandrata, Bernardino Ochino and others carried antitrinitarian opinions into Switzerland, Poland and Transylvania. The details of the meeting are disputed, and the dictionary says so rather than repeating a confident story. What is not disputed is the outcome: Italy produced the men who founded Socinianism, and they came out of the same evangelical reading circles as the orthodox exiles. The dictionary records this plainly because it is the strongest historical case for confessional discipline. A movement that rejects a false church and has no agreed confession of its own will divide over the doctrine of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the Trinity as the union of three persons in one Godhead; a collegium is not in Webster, but a college is a society of persons; a confession as a profession of faith; heterodoxy as an opinion contrary to orthodoxy; and discipline as government by rule.
webster_full: TRINITY, n. The union of three persons in one Godhead, or the three persons of the Father, Son and Holy Ghost in one divine essence.
COLLEGE, n. A collection or assemblage; a society of persons engaged in common pursuits and having common duties.
CONFESSION, n. The acknowledgment of a crime, fault or something that is disadvantageous; a profession of religious faith, or a creed.
HETERODOXY, n. An opinion or doctrine contrary to the true faith or to some established standard.
ORTHODOXY, n. Soundness of faith; a belief in the genuine doctrines taught in the Scriptures.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Venetian city named in 1538 as the second site for the general council, and traditionally the meeting place of the collegium from which Italian antitrinitarianism spread.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is antitrinitarianism itself, and the dictionary names it as an attack on the God who saves rather than as a technical quarrel. The men said to have met at Vicenza objected that the doctrine was not in the words of Scripture; the answer is that the baptismal formula is, and that it is a single name shared by three: go and teach all nations, “baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Mat 28:19). A convert is washed into that name or into nothing.

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is the necessity of a confession. The Italian exiles divided because they had repudiated Rome's authority and had agreed on no standard of their own, and Jude's word assumes precisely such a standard already handed over: believers must “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). Paul calls it a form, an outline of words to be gripped, “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me” (2Ti 1:13). The dictionary holds with the Reformed churches that the three are one, “and these three are one” (1Jo 5:7), and that a church without a subscribed confession has no way to say so when it matters.

pos: n. (the Venetian city of the mainland whose 1577 synod enforced the Tridentine decrees, and a station of the Inquisition on the road from the Alps)
etymology: From Latin Tarvisium, a Veneti town, the name of uncertain sense.
biblical_def: Treviso lies on the Sile north of Venice, the nearest of the mainland cities to the capital and Venetian from 1339. It was an ordinary diocese of the Venetian terra firma, and its interest here is that it shows how the decrees of Trent were actually made to work. The council ended in 1563; what followed was two generations of provincial and diocesan synods, visitations, seminary foundations and parish registers, by which the Roman church became for the first time a uniform teaching institution reaching every village. Treviso held its synod in 1577, founded a seminary, kept registers of baptism, marriage and confession, and worked with the Venetian Holy Office against the few evangelical readers in the trades. The dictionary records Treviso to make a point about machinery. The Reformation was not defeated in Italy by better arguments but by better administration, and Protestants should be sober about that. A confession is not kept by being true; it is kept by being taught, catechised, examined and preached in every parish, year after year, to children.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a parish as the precinct of a church; a register as a book of records; a seminary as a place of education; catechising as instructing by question and answer; and uniformity as consistency with one rule.
webster_full: PARISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the territory committed to one clergyman.
REGISTER, n. A written account or entry of acts, judgments or proceedings, for preserving and conveying the knowledge of them.
SEMINARY, n. A place of education; any school, academy, college or university, in which young persons are instructed.
CATECHISE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions, receiving answers, and offering explanations and corrections.
UNIFORMITY, n. Even tenor; as the uniformity of design in a poem; conformity to one pattern or rule.
scriptures: And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
corruption_summary: Venetian mainland diocese whose 1577 synod, seminary and registers show how Trent's decrees were turned into working parish machinery.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordinary machinery of teaching, which Protestants have often despised as mere routine while losing ground to those who kept it. Trent's administrators were right about method and wrong about doctrine; the Reformed churches at their best were right about both, with catechisms, visitations, presbyteries and examinations before the table. Paul's charge is a command about persistence in season and out: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine” (2Ti 4:2).

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is to treat conviction as self-sustaining. It is not. Jehoshaphat sent teachers from town to town, so that his men “went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people” (2Ch 17:9); Nehemiah's Levites did the exegetical work in public, “and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8); and Luke describes the first church as a body with four fixed habits, continuing “stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42). Treviso teaches by contrast that administration without the gospel is a strong cage; the dictionary wants the gospel and the cage both.

pos: n. (the chief city of Friuli under Venice, and the home of the miller Domenico Scandella, called Menocchio, burned by the Inquisition in 1599)
etymology: From medieval Latin Utinum, of uncertain origin, perhaps from a Friulian root for a height.
biblical_def: Udine is the chief town of Friuli, the Venetian province at the head of the Adriatic where Italian, German and Slavic worlds meet, and it was the seat of the patriarch of Aquileia's administration. Its place in this dictionary is a trial. Domenico Scandella, a miller of Montereale in the Friulian hills, known as Menocchio, was tried by the Inquisition at Udine in 1584 and again in 1599, and burned. He was literate, had read perhaps a dozen books, including a vernacular Bible, a Decameron and a travel account, and had built out of them a cosmology of his own in which the world arose as cheese does from milk and the angels as worms in the cheese. He denied the divinity of Christ as commonly held, doubted the sacraments and thought all religions equally saving. The dictionary records Menocchio with real sympathy and no agreement. He is what happens when a hungry reader gets the Scriptures and nothing else: no church, no catechism, no pastor, no confession. The answer to Menocchio is not fewer books. It is a teaching church.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a miller as one who grinds grain; a heretic as one who holds an error in religion; cosmogony as the generation of the world; vernacular as native to a country; and a pastor as a minister who has the care of a flock.
webster_full: MILLER, n. One whose occupation is to attend a grist-mill, or to grind grain for others.
HERETIC, n. A person under any religion, but particularly the christian, who holds and teaches opinions repugnant to the established faith.
COSMOGONY, n. The generation or creation of the world; the rise or origin of the world or universe.
VERNACULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as a vernacular tongue or idiom.
PASTOR, n. A minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation.
scriptures: Eph 4:11
And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers;
Act 8:31
And he said, How can I, except some man should guide me? And he desired Philip that he would come up and sit with him.

As also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: Friulian capital where the miller Menocchio was tried and burned in 1599 for a homemade cosmology built out of a vernacular Bible and a few other books.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is twofold, and the dictionary refuses to choose between the halves. Rome burned a miller for thinking, which was murder. But Menocchio's opinions were also genuinely false, and the modern habit of celebrating him as a folk philosopher flatters him at the cost of what he actually needed, which was teaching. Peter says of Paul's letters that there are “some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest” (2Pe 3:16). That is a pastoral observation, not a case for withholding the book.

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that the Bible in the hand assumes a ministry alongside it. Christ gave the offices for exactly this purpose, “And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers” (Eph 4:11). The eunuch with the scroll puts the need in a question that answers itself, “How can I, except some man should guide me?” (Act 8:31), and Nehemiah's Levites supply the model of what guiding means, “and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). Sola Scriptura was never solitary Scriptura; the Reformers printed Bibles and catechisms in the same decade, for this reason.

pos: n. (the ancient patriarchate at the head of the Adriatic, seat of Rufinus and of the schism of the Three Chapters, suppressed in 1751)
etymology: From Latin Aquileia, a Roman colony of 181 before Christ, the name perhaps from aquila, an eagle.
biblical_def: Aquileia was one of the great cities of the Roman West and one of the oldest sees in Italy, holding a patriarchate second in Italy only to Rome. Its bishop Valerian presided over the council of Aquileia in 381 which deposed two Arian bishops, with Ambrose of Milan as the moving force. Its priest Rufinus translated Origen, Eusebius and much of the Greek fathers into Latin and wrote the oldest surviving commentary on the Apostles' Creed, which is the earliest witness to that creed in the form the Western church has used since. From 553 Aquileia led the schism of the Three Chapters, refusing the fifth general council's condemnation of three dead writers as a betrayal of Chalcedon; that schism lasted a century and a half. Attila destroyed the city in 452 and its people founded Grado and eventually Venice. The patriarchate was suppressed in 1751 at the demand of Venice and Austria. The dictionary records Aquileia for the Creed, and for the lesson that an ancient and honourable see can be extinguished by two governments in a single stroke.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a creed as a brief summary of the articles of faith; a patriarch as a dignitary superior to archbishops; a schism as a division in a church; translation as the act of rendering into another language; and antiquity as ancient times.
webster_full: CREED, n. A brief summary of the articles of christian faith; a symbol; that which is believed.
PATRIARCH, n. In the christian church, a dignitary superior to the order of archbishops; as the patriarch of Constantinople, of Alexandria, or of Antioch.
SCHISM, n. In a general sense, division or separation; appropriately, a division or separation in a church or denomination of christians.
TRANSLATION, n. The act of turning into another language; the rendering of a discourse or writing into another tongue.
ANTIQUITY, n. Ancient times; former ages; times long since past; the people of ancient times.
scriptures: Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Rom 10:9
That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved.
For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures;
corruption_summary: Ancient Adriatic patriarchate, seat of Rufinus's commentary on the Apostles' Creed and of the century-long schism of the Three Chapters, suppressed in 1751.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the use of a creed, and Aquileia is where the Western church's oldest exposition of one was written. A creed is not a rival to Scripture; it is the church's short answer to the question what the Scriptures teach, and the New Testament already contains such answers in compressed form. Paul hands on a received summary in four clauses, beginning “that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures” (1Co 15:3), and he states the confession a man must make with his mouth, “That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus” (Rom 10:9).

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is the demand for a creedless Christianity on the ground that creeds divide. They do divide, and that is their office: they divide the church from what is not the church. Jude assumes a deposit already fixed when he charges believers to “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3), and Paul calls the thing to be held a form of words rather than a mood, “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus” (2Ti 1:13). Aquileia's long schism also warns the other way: a see may be stubborn about the wrong thing for a hundred and fifty years.

“Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) — a form of words, not a mood.

pos: n. (the Adriatic capital of the late Western empire and of the Gothic and Byzantine exarchate, whose mosaics record the Arian and orthodox churches side by side)
etymology: From Latin Ravenna, of uncertain, probably Etruscan or Umbrian, origin.
biblical_def: Ravenna became the capital of the Western Roman empire in 402 because its marshes made it defensible, and it remained a capital under Odoacer, under the Ostrogothic king Theodoric, and then as the seat of the Byzantine exarch until the Lombards took it in 751. Pepin then gave the territory to the pope, and the Donation of Pepin is the beginning of the papal state. Ravenna's churches preserve what almost nothing else does: an Arian baptistery and an orthodox one, a palace church built by an Arian king and later reconsecrated, and the mosaics of Justinian and Theodora in San Vitale. Theodoric was an Arian ruling a Catholic population and ruled it tolerantly for thirty-three years. The dictionary records Ravenna because the Arian question is not a curiosity: it is whether the one who died is God. The mosaics show two congregations in one city with two answers, and they also show that the tolerant Arian king is remembered gratefully by historians while the doctrine he held, had it prevailed, would have left the church without a Saviour.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Arianism as the doctrine of Arius denying the divinity of Christ; a mosaic as work inlaid with small stones; an exarch as a viceroy or a bishop's deputy; a donation as the act of giving; and consubstantial as of the same substance.
webster_full: ARIANISM, n. The doctrines or tenets of Arius, who denied that Christ was consubstantial with the Father.
MOSAIC, n. A kind of painting in which small pieces of glass, marble or precious stones are inlaid to form figures.
EXARCH, n. A viceroy; in the Greek church, a deputy or legate of a patriarch, who visits the provinces.
DONATION, n. The act of giving or bestowing; a grant; the gift of something to another.
CONSUBSTANTIAL, a. Having the same substance or essence; coessential.
scriptures: Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
Col 2:9
For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
Tit 2:13
Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ;
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: Late imperial and Byzantine capital on the Adriatic whose mosaics preserve Arian and orthodox churches side by side, and the origin of the papal state in 756.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is Arianism, in its ancient form and in the modern versions that reappear whenever the deity of Christ is treated as a late development. The question is not about a word but about who hung on the cross, and Paul settles it in a sentence that no reduced Christ can bear: “For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9). John opens with the same claim about the Word who became flesh, “and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is the practical weight of the doctrine. The church was purchased at a price that the purchaser could only pay if he were God, which is why Paul can describe the flock as that “which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28). The hope believers are taught to wait for is one person described in two words joined, “the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (Tit 2:13). The dictionary gives Theodoric his due as a just ruler and refuses to let that soften the doctrinal verdict. A tolerant heretic is a better neighbour than a cruel orthodox man and still has no gospel to give him.
roots_summary: Greek theotes (G2320), Godhead; Greek logos (G3056), word; Greek peripoieomai (G4046), to purchase.
roots_lines: Greek logos (G3056) — word, reason, utterance; “and the Word was God”, John 1:1.
Greek theotes (G2320) — deity, Godhead, divine nature; “all the fulness of the Godhead bodily”, Colossians 2:9.
Greek pleroma (G4138) — fulness, that which fills; “For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead”, Colossians 2:9.
Greek epiphaneia (G1932) — a shining forth, an appearing; “the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ”, Titus 2:13.
Greek peripoieomai (G4046) — to acquire, to purchase; “which he hath purchased with his own blood”, Acts 20:28.
usage: “and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1) — the claim the Arian baptistery denied.
“For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9) — no reduced Christ can bear it.
“which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28) — why the doctrine has practical weight.

pos: n. (the Adriatic city of the 359 council whose homoean creed produced the Arian high-water mark Jerome described as the world turned Arian)
etymology: From Latin Ariminum, a Roman colony of 268 before Christ, named from the river Ariminus.
biblical_def: Rimini is an Adriatic port at the end of the Flaminian way, and in 359 it was the site of the largest council of the Arian crisis. Constantius the Second summoned the Western bishops to Rimini and the Eastern to Seleucia, intending a single formula for the whole church. About four hundred bishops met at Rimini; the majority stood by Nicaea and deposed the court party, but the emperor refused their deputies, detained them, and wore them down until at Nike in Thrace they subscribed a creed saying that the Son is like the Father, dropping the word of one substance. Constantius then obtained similar subscriptions at Constantinople in 360. Jerome's famous verdict on the moment, that the whole world was made Arian, refers to this. The dictionary records Rimini as the clearest case of a council going wrong by exhaustion rather than by conviction, and as a warning that the number of bishops subscribing a formula settles nothing. Within twenty years the Nicene faith had recovered the whole church, which also says something about how truth survives a majority vote.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a council as an ecclesiastical assembly; subscription as the act of signing one's name; a formula as a prescribed form of words; majority as the greater number; and constancy as firmness of mind.
webster_full: COUNCIL, n. An assembly of ecclesiastics convened for regulating the affairs of the church or determining points of doctrine.
SUBSCRIPTION, n. The act of subscribing or writing one's name underneath; attestation given by underwriting the name.
FORMULA, n. A prescribed form; a rule or model; in theology, a confession of faith reduced to set words.
MAJORITY, n. The greater number; more than half; as a majority of mankind.
CONSTANCY, n. Fixedness; firmness of mind; steadiness; perseverance in a purpose or an opinion.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Pro 28:1
The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.
corruption_summary: Adriatic city of the 359 council whose bishops were worn down into a homoean creed, the moment Jerome described as the world being made Arian.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the authority of a count. Four hundred bishops at Rimini subscribed a formula most of them did not believe, and they did it because an emperor would not let them go home. The lesson is not that councils are useless but that the test of a formula is the text, and Isaiah gives the test without regard to numbers: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). The dictionary applies the same measure to a Protestant assembly and to a papal one.

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is examination followed by grip. Paul's rule is a two-stroke command, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21), and the anathema he pronounces does not spare the highest conceivable authority: “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8). What the worn-down bishops of Rimini lacked was not information but nerve, and Scripture names that too, contrasting the fugitive conscience with the settled one: “but the righteous are bold as a lion” (Pro 28:1). Twenty years later the Nicene faith held the field.
roots_summary: Greek dokimazo (G1381), to test; Greek katecho (G2722), to hold fast; Greek homoousios, of one substance.
roots_lines: Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, to prove by trial; “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good”, 1 Thessalonians 5:21.
Greek katecho (G2722) — to hold down, to retain, to hold fast; “hold fast that which is good”, 1 Thessalonians 5:21.
Greek anathema (G0331) — devoted to destruction, accursed; “let him be accursed”, Galatians 1:8.
Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction; “To the law and to the testimony”, Isaiah 8:20.
Hebrew batach (H0982) — to trust, to be confident; “but the righteous are bold as a lion”, Proverbs 28:1.
usage: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the test a count of bishops cannot replace.
“Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21) — examination followed by grip.
“but the righteous are bold as a lion” (Pro 28:1) — what Rimini's bishops lacked.

pos: n. (the Adriatic port of the papal state, a refuge of Levantine Jews under Paul the Third and the scene of the burnings of 1556 under Paul the Fourth)
etymology: From Greek ankon, an elbow, for the bend of the promontory on which the city stands.
biblical_def: Ancona is the chief Adriatic port of the Marches and from the sixteenth century a city of the papal state. Paul the Third, wanting the trade of the Levant, granted in 1547 a safe conduct inviting Portuguese and Levantine Jews, including conversos who had been baptised under compulsion in Portugal and had resumed Jewish practice abroad, to settle at Ancona with guarantees. Several hundred came. In 1555 Paul the Fourth issued the bull Cum nimis absurdum, establishing the Roman ghetto and revoking the protections; those at Ancona who had been baptised were tried as apostates, and in the spring of 1556 twenty-five were burned and others sent to the galleys. Dona Gracia Nasi organised a boycott of the port from Constantinople in reprisal. The dictionary records Ancona because it is one of the plainest demonstrations in the century that compelled baptism is not baptism, and that a church which first forces a sacrament and then punishes the forced for not keeping it has abandoned the nature of faith altogether.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines baptism as the application of water as a religious rite; apostasy as an abandonment of one's faith; a safe conduct as a convoy or protection granted; compulsion as the act of driving by force; and a ghetto is not in Webster, but a quarter is a district of a town.
webster_full: BAPTISM, n. The application of water to a person, as a sacrament or religious ceremony, by which he is initiated into the visible church of Christ.
APOSTASY, n. An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion or departure from one's faith or religion.
SAFE-CONDUCT, n. That which gives a safe passage; a convoy or guard to protect a person in an enemy's country or in a place of danger.
COMPULSION, n. The act of driving or urging by force, physical or moral; force applied; constraint of the will.
QUARTER, n. A particular region of a town, city or country; as all parts and quarters of the town.
scriptures: For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.
Act 8:36
And as they went on their way, they came unto a certain water: and the eunuch said, See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?
Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
corruption_summary: Adriatic port of the papal state which invited Levantine Jews under safe conduct in 1547 and burned twenty-five of them as apostates in 1556.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is forced profession, and Ancona shows it running its full course from invitation to stake. Men who had been baptised at the point of a decree in Portugal were invited to a papal port under guarantee, and then burned for not holding what had been forced on them. The dictionary says the obvious thing: a sacrament administered to an unwilling adult signifies nothing, because Scripture locates faith in the heart before it reaches the mouth, “For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom 10:10).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that God accepts only what is given freely. The order in Philip's baptism of the eunuch is belief first, on profession, and the eunuch asks for it himself, “See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?” (Act 8:36). Worship must be of a kind that answers to God's own nature, “they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth” (Joh 4:24), and even in the smaller matter of money Paul rules out constraint on a principle that covers the greater: “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2Co 9:7). A church that breaks faith with the people it has guaranteed has also broken it with its own gospel.
roots_summary: Greek homologia from homologeo (G3670), confession; Greek baptizo (G0907), to baptise; Greek anagke (G0318), necessity.
roots_lines: Greek pisteuo (G4100) — to believe, to put trust in; “For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness”, Romans 10:10.
Greek homologeo (G3670) — to confess, to say the same thing; “with the mouth confession is made unto salvation”, Romans 10:10.
Greek baptizo (G0907) — to dip, to immerse, to baptise; “what doth hinder me to be baptized?”, Acts 8:36.
Greek anagke (G0318) — necessity, constraint; “not grudgingly, or of necessity”, 2 Corinthians 9:7.
Greek hilaros (G2431) — cheerful, glad; “for God loveth a cheerful giver”, 2 Corinthians 9:7.
usage: “For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness” (Rom 10:10) — why a forced baptism signifies nothing.
“what doth hinder me to be baptized?” (Act 8:36) — the sacrament asked for, not imposed.
“not grudgingly, or of necessity” (2Co 9:7) — the principle applied to the smaller matter too.

pos: n. (the Ligurian maritime republic, banker to the Spanish crown, whose Oratory of Divine Love shaped the Catholic Reformation)
etymology: From Latin Genua, a Ligurian port, the name perhaps from a root meaning a knee or bend.
biblical_def: Genoa was a maritime republic whose fleets and banks made it indispensable: after 1528 Andrea Doria took the city into the Spanish system, and Genoese bankers financed Charles the Fifth and Philip the Second, carrying the American silver that paid the armies of the Counter-Reformation. Genoa was also the birthplace, about 1497, of the Oratory of Divine Love, a confraternity of clergy and laymen devoted to frequent communion, confession and works of mercy, whose Roman branch included Gaetano da Thiene, Gian Pietro Carafa and Gasparo Contarini. From that circle came the Theatines, the reform commission of 1537, and in time both the irenic wing that hoped for agreement with the Protestants at Regensburg and the rigorist wing that created the Roman Inquisition. The dictionary records Genoa because the two things are connected. A serious devotional revival inside the Roman church produced, within one generation, both the men who negotiated with Melanchthon and the pope who built the ghetto and burned the Jews of Ancona. Piety without a settled doctrine of justification can go either way, and at Genoa it went both.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a republic as a commonwealth; a banker as one who traffics in money; a confraternity as a brotherhood; devotion as solemn attention to God; and rigor as severity of discipline.
webster_full: REPUBLIC, n. A commonwealth; a state in which the supreme power is lodged in the people or their representatives.
BANKER, n. One who keeps a bank; one who traffics in money, receives and remits money, and discounts bills for a profit.
CONFRATERNITY, n. A brotherhood; a society or body of men united for some purpose or in some profession.
DEVOTION, n. A solemn attention to the Supreme Being in worship; the state of being devoted or set apart.
RIGOR, n. Stiffness; strictness; exactness without allowance or indulgence; severity of life or discipline.
scriptures: Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Rom 10:2
For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.
Gal 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
Rom 5:1
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: Ligurian republic and banker to Spain, birthplace of the Oratory of Divine Love from which both the irenic and the rigorist wings of the Catholic Reformation came.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is devotion without a doctrine of acceptance, which the dictionary holds to be unstable by nature. The Genoese Oratory was serious: frequent communion, confession, hospitals, care of incurables. Out of it came Contarini, who at Regensburg in 1541 very nearly agreed a double justification with Melanchthon, and Carafa, who as Paul the Fourth ghettoised the Roman Jews and burned the conversos of Ancona. The same piety served both because it had no fixed answer to the one question, and Paul's word about his own zealous countrymen fits it exactly: “they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. Justification is a verdict already passed, and it is what makes devotion steady instead of anxious: “Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom 5:1). Paul states the article as a conclusion that excludes contribution, “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28), and he treats the liberty that follows as something to be defended rather than enjoyed privately: “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage” (Gal 5:1). The men of the Oratory wanted a holier church. The dictionary says they could not have one without that sentence.
roots_summary: Greek eirene (G1515), peace; Greek eleutheria (G1657), liberty; Greek zelos (G2205), zeal.
roots_lines: Greek eirene (G1515) — peace, a settled state; “we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ”, Romans 5:1.
Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous; “Therefore being justified by faith”, Romans 5:1.
Greek eleutheria (G1657) — liberty, freedom; “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free”, Galatians 5:1.
Greek zugos (G2218) — a yoke, a balance; “and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage”, Galatians 5:1.
Greek zelos (G2205) — zeal, ardour; “they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge”, Romans 10:2.
usage: “they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2) — the Oratory in one line.
“we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom 5:1) — what makes devotion steady.
“Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free” (Gal 5:1) — liberty to be defended, not merely enjoyed.
